summary.text: A self-avoiding walk is a sequence of moves on a lattice that never visits the same point more than once.
It models chain-like molecules such as polymers and proteins, whose physical volume keeps two parts of the chain from sitting in the same spot.
Very little is known rigorously about it, and its properties cannot be calculated analytically, so researchers rely on numerical simulations.

items.prompt: A hiker moves across a city grid, always choosing at random a corner not visited before. What can eventually happen to the hiker?

options.label: Nothing, since there are always unvisited corners nearby
The hiker returns to the first corner automatically
The hiker covers every corner of the grid
The hiker becomes trapped with no empty neighbor

items.explain: In a growing self-avoiding walk, when there are no empty adjacent sites the walk is trapped.

items.prompt: A long chain-like molecule cannot have two parts in the same place. Which kind of walk models its shape better than an ordinary random walk?

options.label: A self-avoiding walk
A walk that doubles back freely
A walk with equal-length steps only
A walk that starts over each step

items.explain: Self-avoiding walks model chain-like entities such as polymers, whose physical volume prohibits multiple occupation of the same point.

items.prompt: A student asks for a formula that counts all self-avoiding walks of a given length on a lattice. What is the honest answer?

options.label: The formula is simple but tedious to apply
There is none known, only rigorous approximations
It is the same count as for ordinary random walks
It was found by chemists studying polymers

items.explain: There is currently no known formula, although there are rigorous methods of approximation.

items.prompt: What name is given to a self-avoiding walk that closes back on itself on a lattice?

options.label: A trapped walk
A lattice loop walk
A pivot walk
A self-avoiding polygon

items.explain: A self-avoiding polygon is a closed self-avoiding walk on a lattice.

items.prompt: Pencil-and-paper formulas cannot give the properties of these walks. How do researchers learn about them instead?

options.label: By running numerical simulations
By tracing the walks by hand on graph paper
By ignoring the self-avoiding rule
By waiting for an exact formula to be found

items.explain: The properties of self-avoiding walks cannot be calculated analytically, so numerical simulations are used.

items.prompt: In four or more dimensions, how is a self-avoiding walk believed to behave?

options.label: It spreads out faster than any other walk
It always ends up trapped quickly
It behaves much like an ordinary random walk
It stops being a walk at all

items.explain: In higher dimensions the self-avoiding walk is believed to behave much like the ordinary random walk, since there is more room to avoid itself.
